hero.name: Nandini
hero.who: a science teacher and mother in Nagpur whose head is crammed with unfinished tasks

story.b: Nandini teaches Class 7 science at a school in Nagpur. It is 2 a.m. and she is wide awake, running through a list in her head. Correct thirty-eight notebooks. Pay the gas bill. Buy a gift for her nephew's birthday on Saturday. Book her mother's eye check-up. Plan the science exhibition. Call the plumber about the dripping tap. Each time she remembers one, another slips away. In the morning she forgets her son's tiffin, and in the staff room she realises the exhibition circular was due yesterday. Her colleague Farzana seems calm with twice the work. Nandini feels like she is carrying a hundred small stones in her head, and dropping one every day.

ask.q: Nandini lies awake listing tasks in her head. What would help her most tonight?
o: Try harder to memorise everything so she stops forgetting things
Write every task and worry down in one place she trusts
Ignore the list and hope she remembers the important ones tomorrow
ask.why: Memory is a poor place to store tasks, which is why they keep circling at night and still get dropped. Ignoring them does not stop the circling. Writing everything down in one trusted place lets her mind stop guarding the list, so she can rest.

chapters.take: Your head is for thinking, not for storing a hundred tasks.

story.b: On Sunday after lunch, Nandini sits on the balcony with a fat notebook and a cup of chai. She sets a timer for ten minutes and writes down everything on her mind, without sorting. Big things, like the exhibition and her mother's eye check-up. Tiny things, like the loose button on her blouse. Worries, like whether her son is happy in his new school. When the timer rings she keeps going for another ten. The final count is sixty-three items. Seeing them all on paper is scary for a moment, then strangely calming. That night she sleeps straight through. On Monday, when a new task pops up in the staff room, she writes it in the notebook instead of holding it.

ask.q: A day later, Nandini's husband reminds her about the car insurance renewal. What should she do with it?
o: Just remember it, since it is only one small item
Put a sticky note on the fridge so she sees it daily
Write it in the same notebook right away
ask.why: One small item seems easy to remember, but that is exactly how her head filled up. A sticky note on the fridge splits her system into many places she must check. Putting it in the one trusted notebook keeps everything together, so her mind can let go.

chapters.take: Capture every task in one trusted place, so your mind can relax.

story.b: Some items on Nandini's list never move. Science exhibition has sat there for a week, and every time she sees it, she feels heavy and looks away. Fix the bathroom tap is the same. One evening she asks a simple question of each stuck item: what is the very next thing I can physically do? For the exhibition, it is asking the school office for the hall booking register. For the tap, it is finding the plumber's number in last year's diary. Written like this, the tasks look almost too small. But the next morning Nandini asks for the register before assembly and books a date. The exhibition stops being a cloud and becomes a list of steps.

ask.q: Her son has Prepare for science olympiad on his list and keeps avoiding it. What should Nandini suggest?
o: Rewrite it as one clear first step, like downloading last year's paper
Remind him every evening that the olympiad is coming soon
Let him wait until he feels more ready to start preparing
ask.why: A vague goal gives no clue where to begin, so the mind avoids it. Reminders add pressure but no direction, and waiting to feel ready can last forever. A clear physical next step, like downloading one paper, makes starting easy, and starting is the hard part.

chapters.take: Vague tasks scare you off. Ask what the very next physical step is.

story.h: Faster to do than to write
story.b: Going through her notebook, Nandini notices something funny. Many items would take less time to do than to write down. Reply to a parent about the field trip. Sign her son's permission slip. Pay the milkman on UPI. Put the gas bill in the bill file. So she makes a new rule. If something will take less than two minutes, she does it now instead of tracking it. In ten minutes she clears nine items. During the school day she applies the same rule. A parent's message gets a one-line reply between periods. A torn chart in the lab gets taped at once. Her list shrinks, and the nagging feeling of loose ends begins to fade.

ask.q: Farzana asks Nandini to confirm a Saturday workshop, a thirty-second reply. What should Nandini do?
o: Add it to her notebook to handle during the weekend
Reply right away, since it takes less time than writing it down
Wait for a free period and answer all her messages together
ask.why: Writing down and later tracking a thirty-second task takes more effort than simply doing it. Waiting lets small tasks pile up into a heavy list. Quick tasks done on the spot keep her list short and her mind clear for the bigger work.

chapters.take: If it takes under two minutes, do it now instead of tracking it.

story.b: Nandini realises some items are not tasks at all but projects, things that need several steps. Her mother's eye check-up needs an appointment, a blood test and a follow-up. The exhibition needs a date, student teams and a budget. Her nephew's birthday needs a gift, a card and a cake order. She makes a short project list, and beside each project she writes its next action. Then she groups the actions by where she can do them: calls, at school, at the computer, and errands in Sitabuldi market. One afternoon she sits in the clinic waiting area for forty minutes. Instead of scrolling, she opens her calls list and phones the cake shop, the plumber and the bus contractor.

ask.q: Nandini is going to Sitabuldi market for one errand. How can her lists help her most?
o: Check her errands list and finish every task that can be done there
Buy only the one item, so she does not get distracted
Ask her husband what else might be needed at home
ask.why: Grouping tasks by place means that whenever she is in the right spot, she knows exactly what can be done there. Doing one item wastes the trip, and asking around depends on someone else's memory. Her errands list turns one outing into several finished tasks.

chapters.take: Group next steps by place, so every place tells you what you can do.

story.b: By the third week, Nandini's notebook is getting messy. Crossed-out lines, half-done projects, a loose bill tucked inside. She catches herself remembering things in her head again, because she is no longer sure the notebook is up to date. So she blocks thirty minutes every Saturday morning, before the vegetable shopping. She empties her school bag and her saved messages, crosses out what is done, updates each project's next action and checks the calendar for the next two weeks. Ideas she likes but cannot do now, like learning Marathi calligraphy or a trip with college friends, go onto a separate someday list. She closes the notebook feeling caught up, even though the work is not finished.

ask.q: One Saturday Nandini is tired and wants to skip her weekly review. What is the wisest choice?
o: Skip it, since her notebook is already full of tasks
Skip it this month and review everything properly in the holidays
Do a short version so the notebook stays current and trusted
ask.why: The system only works while she trusts it, and trust comes from regular review. Skipping for weeks lets the notebook drift out of date until her head takes over again. A short review, even fifteen minutes, keeps it current, so her mind can stay calm.

chapters.take: A system you review every week is a system you can trust.

story.b: The science exhibition opens on a Friday in December, and Nandini walks through the hall checking stalls instead of running around with a racing heart. The bus came on time, the chart paper arrived on Tuesday, and her mother's eye check-up happened two weeks ago. She still has plenty to do. The difference is that it lives in her notebook, not in her head. Quick replies happen at once, stuck items become first steps, and Saturday mornings begin with her thirty-minute review. Farzana asks for her secret. Nandini shows her the plain notebook and laughs at how ordinary it looks. That night she falls asleep by eleven, and nothing circles in her head.

chapters.take: When everything lives in a trusted system, your mind is free to do the work.
